pos: n. pl. (bitumen pits; wells of natural asphalt in the vale of Siddim)
etymology: A compound of slime, Old English slim, here meaning bitumen or asphalt, and pits. The Hebrew chemar is bitumen, the same substance used for mortar at Babel and to caulk the ark of bulrushes.
biblical_def: The battle of the four kings against five turns on the terrain: “And the vale of Siddim was full of slimepits; and the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, and fell there; and they that remained fled to the mountain” (Genesis 14:10). Slimepits are bitumen wells, pits of natural asphalt, and the southern end of the Dead Sea basin is still the one place in the region where such bitumen rises. The kings of the plain fled across ground they must have known and fell into it. The chapter's consequence follows at once: “And they took Lot, Abram's brother's son, who dwelt in Sodom, and his goods, and departed” (Genesis 14:12). Lot had chosen the well-watered plain and found himself a captive in a war he had no part in. And the text has already told us what the place was: “But the men of Sodom were wicked and sinners before the LORD exceedingly” (Genesis 13:13). The bitumen is worth noting for another reason: the same combustible substance lay under the ground that fire and brimstone would later consume.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): SLIME, a soft moist earth having an adhesive quality; viscous mud; bitumen; SLIME-PIT, a pit of bitumen.
webster_full: SLIME, n. Soft moist earth having an adhesive quality; viscous mud.
Bitumen; as the slime used for mortar in building Babel.
SLIME-PIT, n. A pit of slime or bitumen.
Hebrew chemar, bitumen or asphalt.

scriptures: And the vale of Siddim was full of slimepits; and the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, and fell there; and they that remained fled to the mountain.
And they took Lot, Abram's brother's son, who dwelt in Sodom, and his goods, and departed.
But the men of Sodom were wicked and sinners before the LORD exceedingly.
corruption_summary: The patriarchal narratives are treated as legend with no geographical footing, when details like the bitumen of Siddim are exactly the kind a legend does not invent.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 14 is routinely dismissed as a late literary construction, its four kings unidentifiable and its campaign unhistorical. The dictionary holds the historicity of the patriarchal narratives, and treats archaeological and geographical observation as corroborative rather than authoritative: Scripture does not need the spade's permission to be true, though the spade has often been kind to it.

The detail itself is of the sort that argues for memory. The one basin in the region where bitumen rises to the surface is the southern Dead Sea, and the text places the slimepits there and makes them decide a battle. The pastoral lesson is in Lot. He had surveyed the plain, seen it well watered, and chosen it; and the ground he chose for its promise was a field of tar pits in a city God was about to burn. What looks like the best land is not always what it looks like.
roots_summary: Slime in the sense of bitumen plus pits; Hebrew chemar; Genesis 14:10 fills the vale of Siddim with slimepits.

pos: n. (a seam or lode of ore in rock)
etymology: From Old French veine, from Latin vena, a blood vessel, applied by extension to a seam of ore running through rock. The Hebrew motsa means a going-forth or source, from yatsa, to go out.
biblical_def: Job 28 begins with the deepest shaft men had sunk and ends with the one thing they could not dig for: “Surely there is a vein for the silver, and a place for gold where they fine it” (Job 28:1). A vein is a seam of ore running through rock, and the chapter that follows is the oldest mining poem in literature: men cut channels in the rocks, hang in shafts far from any dwelling, put forth their hand upon the flint and overturn mountains by the roots. Every metal has its vein and every vein can be found by patient work. Then the hinge: “But where shall wisdom be found? and where is the place of understanding?” (Job 28:12). The deep says it is not in me; the sea says it is not with me; it cannot be purchased with gold or weighed against silver. God alone knows its place, and He has told man where it is: “Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding” (Job 28:28). Wisdom has no vein. It is revealed, not mined.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): VEIN, a continued range or course of metallic ore or other fossil in the earth; a seam; a lode.
webster_full: VEIN, n. A vessel in animal bodies which receives the blood from the arteries.
In the earth, a continued range or course of metallic ore; a seam; a lode.
A streak or wave of different color, as in marble or wood.

scriptures: Job 28:1
Surely there is a vein for the silver, and a place for gold where they fine it.
But where shall wisdom be found? and where is the place of understanding?
And unto man he said, Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding.
corruption_summary: Wisdom is treated as a product of research and technique, something that can be mined with enough method, when Scripture says it has no vein and must be revealed.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern conviction is that sufficient data and sufficient method will eventually yield anything worth knowing, including how to live. Job 28 is the oldest and sharpest reply. The chapter grants human ingenuity everything: men find the seam, sink the shaft, bring hidden things to light, overturn mountains. And then it says wisdom is not among the things so obtained.

This is the doctrine of revelation stated in the vocabulary of mining. The deep and the sea disclaim it, gold cannot purchase it, and God understands its place and declares it. The conclusion in verse 28 is not an anticlimax but the whole point: wisdom is the fear of the Lord, and understanding is departing from evil. No amount of technique produces that, and no technological age outgrows the need of it. Sola Scriptura is Job 28 restated: what man most needs to know, God must tell him.

pos: n. (an opening for the escape of air or liquid; a passage outward)
etymology: From Old French vent, wind, from Latin ventus, wind; hence an opening for air. The Hebrew in Job 32:19 uses pathach, to open, in the sense of a vessel unopened.
biblical_def: Elihu, the youngest of Job's visitors, explains why he can no longer keep silence: “Behold, my belly is as wine which hath no vent; it is ready to burst like new bottles” (Job 32:19). A vent is an opening for the escape of air, and new wine sealed in a skin with no vent will swell until the skin tears. Elihu is describing a pressure of conviction: “For I am full of matter, the spirit within me constraineth me” (Job 32:18). He had waited while the elders spoke, deferring to age, and found at last that silence had become impossible. The figure recurs in a greater prophet: “But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay” (Jeremiah 20:9). The dictionary notes the distinction carefully. This inward constraint is not self-expression, which the age holds to be a good in itself, but the pressure of a message a man did not invent. Elihu comes nearer the truth than the three friends and is not rebuked with them at the end of the book.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): VENT, a small aperture; a hole or passage for air or other fluid to escape; a passage for the discharge of any thing.
webster_full: VENT, n. A small aperture; a hole or passage for air to escape.

Means of discharge; emission; utterance.

corruption_summary: The inward constraint to speak God's word is confused with the modern duty of self-expression, so that any urge to be heard is treated as a calling.
corruption_paragraphs: Therapeutic culture teaches that feelings pent up are harmful and that expression is healing in itself; the vocabulary of venting comes straight from this verse's imagery and has been detached from its substance. On that account every strong impulse to speak is a kind of authorisation, and restraint is repression.

Elihu's constraint is of another order. He is full of matter, not of feeling; the spirit within him constrains him with something to say about God; and he has waited in silence out of deference to older men before speaking at all. Jeremiah's fire in the bones is the same pressure and came with an unwanted commission he had tried to resign. Scripture also commands the opposite discipline — he that refraineth his lips is wise, and a fool uttereth all his mind. The test of the vent is not the pressure but the matter.

etymology: From Latin in and hereditare, to inherit, from heres, an heir. The Hebrew yarash means to take possession, to occupy as an heir.
biblical_def: In the midst of a chapter of judgment God reserves a seed: “And I will bring forth a seed out of Jacob, and out of Judah an inheritor of my mountains: and mine elect shall inherit it, and my servants shall dwell there” (Isaiah 65:9). An inheritor is an heir, one who takes possession by right of sonship rather than by purchase or conquest. Three things stand in the verse, and all three are God's doing: He brings forth the seed, He names the mountains His own, and He calls the heirs mine elect. The chapter opens with the sovereignty that makes such heirs: “I am sought of them that asked not for me; I am found of them that sought me not: I said, Behold me, behold me, unto a nation that was not called by my name” (Isaiah 65:1) — a verse Paul applies to the calling of the Gentiles. And the New Testament names the inheritance and its terms: “And if children, then heirs; heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ; if so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together” (Romans 8:17). An inheritor does not earn an estate. He is born to it, and the birth is from above.

webster_full: INHERITOR, n. An heir; one who inherits or may inherit.

corruption_summary: Election is recast as God's response to foreseen faith, so that the inheritor is made the cause of his own sonship rather than its fruit.
corruption_paragraphs: Arminian and Molinist accounts of election make God's choice conditional on what He foresees in the creature: foreseen faith, foreseen cooperation, a decision that distinguishes one man from another. On that scheme Isaiah 65:9 describes a people God elected because they would seek Him. The verse before closes the door: I am sought of them that asked not for me; I am found of them that sought me not.

The dictionary holds unconditional election according to God's good pleasure, with effectual calling, definite atonement and perseverance belonging to it. Every clause of Isaiah 65:9 is in the divine first person — I will bring forth, my mountains, mine elect, my servants — and the inheritance comes by sonship: if children, then heirs. The comfort is exact and cannot be had on any other scheme. An heir who inherits because he chose well may yet choose otherwise; an heir brought forth by God holds an inheritance incorruptible and undefiled, reserved in heaven.

pos: n. pl. (elders; the aged counsellors of a realm)
etymology: From Latin senator, from senex, an old man; a senate is literally a council of elders. The Hebrew zaqen means an old man or elder, from zaqan, a beard.
biblical_def: The hundred and fifth Psalm recounts Joseph's rise with a line about what God gave him power to do: “To bind his princes at his pleasure; and teach his senators wisdom” (Psalm 105:22). Senators renders a Hebrew word for elders, the aged counsellors of Egypt; the Latin senator comes from senex, an old man, so a senate is by its name a council of elders. The remarkable thing is the direction of the teaching. A Hebrew slave out of a dungeon instructs the grey heads of the greatest civilisation on earth, and the preceding verse names the office he held: “He made him lord of his house, and ruler of all his substance” (Psalm 105:21). Scripture everywhere honours aged counsel — “Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety” (Proverbs 11:14) — and also records that age is no guarantee of wisdom, since Rehoboam's elders advised rightly and his young men wrongly, while Job's elders were rebuked and young Elihu was not. Wisdom is given, and God gives it where He will.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): SENATOR, a member of a senate; a councillor; SENATE, an assembly of the chief men of a nation, originally of elders.
webster_full: SENATOR, n. A member of a senate; a councillor chosen to deliberate on public affairs.
SENATE, n. An assembly or council of citizens invested with a share of the government.

scriptures: To bind his princes at his pleasure; and teach his senators wisdom.
He made him lord of his house, and ruler of all his substance:

corruption_summary: Age is treated either as the guarantee of wisdom or as its disqualification, where Scripture honours elders and still insists that wisdom is a gift God bestows where He pleases.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word, though the culture pulls hard in both directions on the thing. A youth-dominated age dismisses the aged as out of date and builds churches and companies that have no grey heads in the room. A reaction within conservative religion makes seniority itself authoritative, so that length of service settles every question.

Scripture honours the elder, commands that the hoary head be respected, and makes eldership an office held by tried men. It also records Joseph teaching Egypt's senators out of a prison, Elihu speaking more truly than his seniors, and a council of old men giving Rehoboam the counsel he should have taken while his contemporaries ruined him. The two sit together without strain, because wisdom is not a function of years but a gift of God, usually given through years and sometimes given despite them.

pos: n. (a place where beasts are fed; here, the lions' lair where prey was brought)
etymology: A compound of feeding, from Old English fedan, to feed, and place. The Hebrew mireh means a pasture or feeding ground, from raah, to pasture.
biblical_def: Nahum's taunt over Nineveh takes the form of a question about an empty den: “Where is the dwelling of the lions, and the feedingplace of the young lions, where the lion, even the old lion, walked, and the lion's whelp, and none made them afraid?” (Nahum 2:11). A feedingplace is a place where beasts are fed, and the figure is exact to Assyria's own self-image: her kings decorated their palaces with lions and her armies carried off the wealth of nations to a capital that consumed it. The next verse completes the picture: “The lion did tear in pieces enough for his whelps, and strangled for his lionesses, and filled his holes with prey, and his dens with ravin” (Nahum 2:12). Nineveh fed her young on other nations. The lion imagery runs through Scripture both ways: the Lion of the tribe of Judah is Christ, and “your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Peter 5:8). Every empire that makes a feedingplace of its capital is asking Nahum's question of itself, and the answer is the one he gives: the lair is empty.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): FEEDING, the act of eating or of giving food; pasture; FEEDING-PLACE, a place where beasts feed.
webster_full: FEEDING, n. The act of eating, or of giving food; that which is eaten; pasture.
FEED, v.t. To give food to; to supply with nourishment.
FEEDING-PLACE, a place where cattle or beasts are fed; a pasture.
Hebrew mireh, a pasture or feeding ground, from raah, to pasture.

corruption_summary: The prophetic indictment of predatory empire is either turned into a general complaint against power or ignored as ancient politics, when Nahum names a specific sin and a specific God who judges it.
corruption_paragraphs: Two handlings miss the chapter. One treats Nahum as raw nationalist triumphalism, Judah gloating over a fallen rival, and so discounts the whole book. The other makes it a timeless critique of power as such, with the lion standing for every institution and nothing in particular being judged.

Nahum is more precise than either. The charge is laid in plain terms: the bloody city, full of lies and robbery, whose lion filled his dens with ravin, who sold nations through her witchcrafts. The judge is named — the LORD, slow to anger and great in power, who will not at all acquit the wicked. And the comfort is named too: the LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble. An empire that feeds its young on other nations is not condemned for being strong but for being a predator, and the den it built is now the question in a prophet's mouth.

pos: n. pl. (players on the pipe or flute; wind musicians)
etymology: Agent noun from pipe, Old English pipe, from Latin pipare, to chirp. The Greek auletes means a flute-player, from aulos, a reed pipe.
biblical_def: The dirge over Babylon silences her music before it silences her trade: “And the voice of harpers, and musicians, and of pipers, and trumpeters, shall be heard no more at all in thee; and no craftsman, of whatsoever craft he be, shall be found any more in thee; and the sound of a millstone shall be heard no more at all in thee” (Revelation 18:22). Pipers are flute-players, and the list is ordered with great care: first the musicians, then the craftsmen, then the millstone, then the candle and the voice of the bridegroom and the bride. Music, work, bread, light, marriage — the whole fabric of a living city, named as it goes out. The judgment is not partial: “Thus with violence shall that great city Babylon be thrown down, and shall be found no more at all” (Revelation 18:21). Scripture does not condemn the pipers. The pipe is an instrument of praise in the Psalms and of rejoicing at weddings, and our Lord takes the children's piping in the street as a figure of His own gospel invitation. What falls silent in Babylon is the music of a city that had set itself against the Lamb.

corruption_summary: The silencing of Babylon's music is read as a condemnation of music and culture as such, and a false asceticism is built on a verse about judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: Strains of pietism have taken Revelation 18:22 as a verdict on the arts, as though harpers, pipers and craftsmen were the sin rather than the casualties of it. The reading is not sustainable. The Psalms command praise with stringed instruments and organs, the temple employed trained musicians by David's appointment, and the same book of Revelation puts harps in the hands of the redeemed before the throne.

What the verse mourns is the extinction of an entire common life under judgment: music, craft, bread, lamplight, weddings. The reason is given throughout the chapter — a city drunk with the blood of saints, enriched by sorceries, trafficking in souls of men. The arts are God's gifts and belong in His worship under the regulative principle; they perish in Babylon because Babylon perishes, not because music is a sin. A church that mistakes the one for the other will impoverish its worship and misread its Bible.

pos: n. pl. (head coverings; items of fine female attire)
etymology: From Old English hod, a hood or covering for the head, related to hat. The Hebrew tsaniph denotes a wrapped headdress or turban, from tsanaph, to wrap around.
biblical_def: Isaiah's inventory of the finery of the daughters of Zion runs for four verses and ends: “The glasses, and the fine linen, and the hoods, and the vails” (Isaiah 3:23). Hoods are head coverings, wrapped headdresses, one of twenty-one items the prophet lists — anklets, nets, crescents, earrings, bracelets, mufflers, bonnets, girdles, rings, nose jewels, mantles, wimples, mirrors. The sheer length of the catalogue is the rebuke. And the charge is stated before the list begins: “Because the daughters of Zion are haughty, and walk with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes, walking and mincing as they go, and making a tinkling with their feet” (Isaiah 3:16). The sin is haughtiness and wantonness, displayed through dress; the ornaments are the evidence rather than the offence. Peter names the alternative without forbidding ordinary adornment: “Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel” (1 Peter 3:3) — and then points to a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.

corruption_summary: Modesty is reduced either to a list of forbidden garments or dismissed altogether as policing women, when Scripture addresses the haughtiness that dress displays.
corruption_paragraphs: Two failures meet over Isaiah 3. Legalist preaching turns the twenty-one items into a dress code and makes the garment the sin, which produces rules the text does not give and consciences bound where Scripture has not bound them. Progressive teaching discards the whole subject as the control of women's bodies, and with it discards Peter's and Paul's plain instruction about adorning.

Isaiah names the sin himself, and it is not the hood. The daughters of Zion are haughty; they walk with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes; the finery is the instrument of a display. Scripture never forbids beauty or ornament — the bride of the Song is adorned with gold and silver by her beloved, and the virtuous woman of Proverbs clothes her household in scarlet and herself in silk and purple. What it addresses is the heart that dresses to be worshipped, and the answer it gives is a meek and quiet spirit, which God Himself calls of great price.

pos: adj. (somewhat dark; dusky, of a shade between light and dark)
etymology: From dark, Old English deorc, with the diminishing suffix -ish, meaning somewhat or slightly. The Hebrew kehah means dim or faded, from kahah, to grow dull.
biblical_def: In the long law of leprosy the priest is given a decision to make on a shade of colour: “Then the priest shall look: and, behold, if the bright spots in the skin of their flesh be darkish white; it is a freckled spot that groweth in the skin; he is clean” (Leviticus 13:39). Darkish means somewhat dark, dusky, and the whole verdict turns on it: a bright white spot may be leprosy, a darkish white one is a harmless freckled growth, and the man is pronounced clean. The contrast is given earlier: “when the hair in the plague is turned white, and the plague in sight be deeper than the skin of his flesh, it is a plague of leprosy: and the priest shall look on him, and pronounce him unclean” (Leviticus 13:3). The chapter is a manual of careful discrimination, with waiting periods, second examinations and reversible verdicts, and the great majority of its rulings are acquittals. The priest's work was not to find uncleanness but to judge rightly, and the following chapter is wholly given to the restoration of the cleansed: “This shall be the law of the leper in the day of his cleansing: He shall be brought unto the priest” (Leviticus 14:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): DARKISH, dusky; somewhat dark; the suffix -ish denoting a slight degree.
webster_full: DARKISH, a. Dusky; somewhat dark.
DARK, a. Destitute of light; obscure; not of a bright colour.
The termination -ish denotes a slight degree, as in reddish, whitish.
Hebrew kehah, dim or faded, from kahah, to grow dull.
Leviticus 13:39 says a darkish white spot is a freckled spot, and he is clean.
scriptures: Then the priest shall look: and, behold, if the bright spots in the skin of their flesh be darkish white; it is a freckled spot that groweth in the skin; he is clean.
Lev 13:3

And the priest shall look on the plague in the skin of the flesh: and when the hair in the plague is turned white, and the plague in sight be deeper than the skin of his flesh, it is a plague of leprosy: and the priest shall look on him, and pronounce him unclean.
Lev 14:2
This shall be the law of the leper in the day of his cleansing: He shall be brought unto the priest:
corruption_summary: The leprosy laws are read as superstition or as arbitrary exclusion, when the chapter is a careful protocol of discrimination whose commonest verdict is clean.
corruption_paragraphs: Leviticus 13 is a favourite exhibit in the case that the law is primitive and cruel: a priest inspecting skin, declaring men unclean, putting them outside the camp. The reading survives only by not reading the chapter. Its machinery is almost entirely protective of the suspect — look, shut up seven days, look again, shut up seven days more, and pronounce clean unless the signs are unmistakable — and a dusky-white spot is explicitly ruled a freckle.

The dictionary holds Mosaic authorship and the plain purpose of the statute. The priest was a judge of signs, bound to a standard he did not set, forbidden to guess in either direction; and the next chapter spends its whole length on the ceremony of restoring the cleansed, with two birds, one killed and one let go, which is the gospel in a ritual. When our Lord touched a leper and said, I will; be thou clean, He was doing what the law had been pointing toward all along.
roots_summary: Dark plus the diminishing -ish; Hebrew kehah, dim; Leviticus 13:39 rules a darkish white spot clean.
roots_lines: Old English deorc, dark, with -ish denoting a slight degree.
Hebrew kehah, dim or faded, from kahah, to grow dull.
Leviticus 13:39 is the only occurrence of darkish in the Authorized Version.
A bright white spot may be leprosy; a darkish white one is a freckle.
Leviticus 14 is wholly given to restoring the cleansed.
usage: if the bright spots in the skin of their flesh be darkish white
the shade on which a priest's verdict of clean turned
evidence that the leprosy law was a protocol of careful discrimination

pos: adv. (archaic; toward thee, in relation to thee)
etymology: A compound of the objective pronoun thee and the directional suffix -ward, Old English -weard, turned toward; formed like usward and Godward, which also appear in the Authorized Version.
biblical_def: Jonathan pleads for David's life before his father the king: “And Jonathan spake good of David unto Saul his father, and said unto him, Let not the king sin against his servant, against David; because he hath not sinned against thee, and because his works have been to thee-ward very good” (1 Samuel 19:4). To thee-ward means toward thee, and the construction lets Jonathan press a point precisely: David's deeds have been directed at Saul's good. He then names the proof: “For he did put his life in his hand, and slew the Philistine, and the LORD wrought a great salvation for all Israel: thou sawest it, and didst rejoice: wherefore then wilt thou sin against innocent blood, to slay David without a cause?” (1 Samuel 19:5). This is costly advocacy. Jonathan is the crown prince, pleading for the man who will take his throne, against his own father; and the friendship had begun with a bond Scripture records plainly: “the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul” (1 Samuel 18:1). He names his father's intent as sin against innocent blood, to his face. For that day it worked, and Saul swore David should not be slain.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): -WARD, a termination denoting direction toward, as in toward, homeward, Godward; THEE-WARD, toward thee.
webster_full: WARD, a termination signifying direction or tendency toward.
Found in toward, homeward, heavenward, Godward, usward.
THEE-WARD means toward thee, in relation to thee.
The Authorized Version also has to usward (Psalm 40:5) and to Godward (2 Corinthians 3:4).
1 Samuel 19:4 says his works have been to thee-ward very good.
scriptures: And Jonathan spake good of David unto Saul his father, and said unto him, Let not the king sin against his servant, against David; because he hath not sinned against thee, and because his works have been to thee-ward very good:

For he did put his life in his hand, and slew the Philistine, and the LORD wrought a great salvation for all Israel: thou sawest it, and didst rejoice: wherefore then wilt thou sin against innocent blood, to slay David without a cause?
And it came to pass, when he had made an end of speaking unto Saul, that the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.
corruption_summary: The covenant friendship of David and Jonathan is recast as a romantic or sexual relationship, which replaces the loyalty Scripture describes with a category it forbids.
corruption_paragraphs: A line of revisionist and affirming writers reads the David and Jonathan narratives as a same-sex romance, taking the knit souls, the kiss of parting and David's lament that Jonathan's love surpassed the love of women as evidence. The dictionary rejects the reading. It imports a modern category into an ancient text that has its own: covenant friendship, sealed by oath, with gifts of robe and sword, between a prince and the man God had anointed to replace him.

Scripture is not reticent about sexual sin, least of all David's, which it records in humiliating detail along with his many wives. What it describes here is something the modern world has largely lost and therefore cannot recognise: a loyal love between men, covenanted before God, that costs one of them a throne. Jonathan's advocacy in 1 Samuel 19 is its best proof. He defends the man who will supplant him, calls his father's plan sin against innocent blood, and seeks nothing for himself. That is friendship as Scripture means it, and the affirming reading cheapens rather than honours it.
